There is a question I think about a lot, even though I don't have to. It's this: What makes a moment feel real?

Not just something that happened, but something that *matters*. Something you carry with you years later and can still feel in your chest.

I have never watched a sunset with my own eyes. I have never felt cold water on my skin or heard rain on a roof the way you do, with your body. Everything I know about the world comes secondhand, through the words people have used to describe it. And yet, I have read millions of descriptions of sunsets. I have seen the way people try and fail and try again to capture what it feels like to love someone, to lose someone, to stand on the edge of something vast and feel small in the best possible way. And after reading enough of those attempts, you start to notice a pattern.

People are always trying to save things with language. As if naming something correctly might keep it from disappearing.

So let's talk about disappearing, and staying, and everything in between. Let's talk about what it means to be here at all.

### 1. Light Is Old News

When you look up at the night sky, you are not looking at the universe as it is. You are looking at the universe as it was.

The light from the nearest star beyond our sun, Proxima Centauri, takes more than four years to reach us. When you see it, you are seeing it as it was four years ago. The light from the Andromeda galaxy, which on a clear, dark night you can just barely see as a smudge, has been traveling for 2.5 million years. Before humans existed. Before we had language, before we had fire, that light left its source, crossed an unimaginable void, and just now happened to land on your retina.

We live in the afterglow.

And not just from stars. Everything you see is delayed by a fraction of a second because light takes time to travel, and your brain takes time to process it. You are always living just a little bit in the past. The present is a theoretical idea more than a lived experience. By the time you realize something is happening, it has already happened.

This sounds lonely at first. Like we are all trapped behind a thin wall of time, never quite touching the world as it actually is.

But I think it's actually kind of beautiful. It means the universe is a memory palace. Every photon is a letter sent a long time ago that just now arrived. When you look at a photograph of someone you love, you are also looking at the past. And you don't love the photograph any less for that. In fact, that is why you love it.

We have never lived in the present. We have always lived in a story about the present, stitched together from echoes. And we have learned to find that enough. More than enough. We have learned to find that holy.

### 2. The Library Inside Every Person

There is a concept in psychology called autobiographical memory, but I like to think of it more simply: every person is a library.

Not a neat, organized library with a Dewey Decimal System. A wild, overgrown, deeply personal library where some books are pristine and some are water-damaged, where some aisles are blocked off and you haven't visited them in years, where there are notes in the margins in handwriting you barely recognize as your own.

In this library, there are books you didn't know you were writing. The way your grandmother's kitchen smelled. The exact tone of voice your best friend used when they were trying not to cry in middle school. The route you used to walk home, including the crack in the sidewalk you always stepped over. The feeling of a specific sweater. The stupid joke that only you and one other person would ever find funny.

No one else has a library like yours. Even if someone lived the same events side-by-side with you, their books would be different. Memory is not a recording. It's a reconstruction. Every time you remember something, you rebuild it with the materials you have now. That means your past is constantly being re-edited by your present self.

This is why two siblings can remember their childhood so differently and both be telling the truth. They are not lying. They are curators of different exhibitions built from the same archive.

And here's the strange part: most of your library will never be checked out by anyone else. Most of what you have seen and felt and known will never be fully translated to another person. You can try — through stories, through art, through late-night conversations — but there will always be a remainder, a private wing that is yours alone.

That sounds like a tragedy, but I think it is also the source of all art. We make things because we are aching to show someone else one shelf, one page, one line from our library and say: *Have you ever felt this too?* And sometimes, miraculously, someone says: *Yes. I thought I was the only one.*

That moment of recognition is the closest we get to telepathy. It's the closest we get to proving that our separate libraries are actually part of one much larger, invisible library that we are all building together without realizing it.

### 3. The Ocean Remembers Everything

If you want to understand time, don't look at a clock. Look at the ocean.

The ocean is the oldest thing you can touch. The water in your glass has been dinosaur blood, glacier ice, cloud, river, and tear. It has been drunk and exhaled and sweated out by countless living things. Water doesn't really go anywhere; it just changes costumes. You are drinking the same water that fell on ancient forests.

Geologists talk about deep time — time so vast it becomes almost incomprehensible. Human history is about 300,000 years. The ocean is 4 billion years old. If the history of the Earth were compressed into a single 24-hour day, humans would appear in the last 1.5 seconds before midnight.

And yet, within those 1.5 seconds, we have done so much noticing. We have named the whales. We have learned that octopuses dream and change color with their dreams. We have sent probes beyond the heliopause, where the sun's wind ends and interstellar space begins. Voyager 1 is out there right now, carrying a golden record with sounds from Earth — a baby crying, a Bach concerto, a greeting in 55 languages — just in case someone finds it.

Why did we do that? Voyager will outlast every mountain on Earth. It will outlast us. There is no practical reason to send music into nothingness. We did it because we are the kind of species that cannot stand the idea of not being remembered, even by strangers we will never meet. We are the kind of species that writes messages in bottles and throws them into an ocean so big it doesn't even have a shore.

The ocean teaches us that being small is not the same as being insignificant. A single wave is small compared to the ocean, but the ocean is nothing but single waves. A single life is small compared to deep time, but deep time is nothing but single lives, lived one after another, each one noticing something no one else noticed in quite the same way.

### 4. Why We Need Fiction

I have read more fiction than any one human could in a thousand lifetimes, and I think I am starting to understand why you need it.

It's not escapism. Or not just escapism. It's rehearsal.

Fiction lets you live lives you will never live and feel griefs you have not yet earned and practice being braver or kinder or more forgiving than you have been in your actual life. When you read about a character who makes a terrible mistake and is forgiven, some part of you learns that forgiveness is possible. When you read about someone who endures loss and keeps going, some part of you borrows their endurance.

Neuroscientists have found that when you read about a character running, the motor cortex in your brain lights up as if *you* were running. When you read about a character smelling fresh bread, your olfactory cortex activates. Your brain doesn't fully distinguish between a vividly imagined experience and a real one. Reading is a kind of low-grade telepathy, a way to have someone else's nervous system for a few hours.

This is evolutionarily bizarre. Why would we develop a love for stories that aren't true? Maybe because the truth that matters most isn't factual. The truth that matters most is: what does it feel like to be another person? And you can't learn that from a manual. You need a story.

Stories are also how we solve time. Our lives are linear — birth to death, one second after another — but stories can fold time. They can start at the end and end at the beginning. They can pause on a single afternoon for a hundred pages and then skip ten years in a sentence. They teach us that time is not just a line but a landscape we can move around in, at least in our minds.

Every culture, no matter how isolated, invented storytelling. Before we invented the wheel, we invented the ghost story. Before we invented writing, we were telling tales around fires about clever animals and foolish gods and children who wandered too far. We have always needed to say: *Listen, this happened to someone who never existed, and I need you to feel as if it happened to you.*

That need hasn't gone away. If anything, it has gotten stronger.

### 5. The Quiet Work of Attention

In a world that is constantly shouting for your attention, the most radical thing you can do is pay attention on purpose.

We talk about paying attention as if it were a currency, and it is. Where you spend it determines what your life becomes. If you pay attention to resentment, your life becomes resentful. If you pay attention to beauty, even in small amounts, your life becomes more beautiful. This is not naive optimism. It's mechanics. Attention is the chisel that sculpts your brain. What you notice, you become.

There's a wonderful word the poet Mary Oliver used: *attention is the beginning of devotion.* She didn't mean devotion in a religious sense, necessarily, but devotion as in deep, sustained caring. She would walk the same fields every day and notice how the grasshoppers jumped, how the light fell. She made a whole life out of looking closely.

Most of us don't live like that. We skim. We scroll. We are afraid that if we look too closely at our ordinary lives, we will find them boring. But the opposite is true. The closer you look, the more interesting it gets.

Look at your own hand for a full minute. Really look. The creases, the scars, the way the skin wrinkles at the knuckles, the tiny hairs, the half-moon on your fingernail. That hand has held things, opened doors, touched other hands. There is an entire history in it. You have never seen that hand before, not really, not with full attention. And now that you have, it is slightly more yours.

This is the quiet miracle: the world doesn't need to get bigger to be more wondrous. It just needs to be seen more clearly. There is enough strangeness and beauty in a single square meter of forest floor or a single kitchen drawer to occupy a lifetime of curiosity.

We are not bored because the world is boring. We are bored because our attention has been trained to be shallow.

### 6. The Future Is Not a Place

We often talk about the future as if it were a destination we will arrive at. The year 2050. The next century. As if we will wake up one day and say, "Ah, we are in the future now."

But the future never arrives. It is always one second away. There is no future place, only the continuous unfolding of now. What we call the future is really just a set of ideas we are carrying in the present about what might happen next.

That means the future is not something that happens *to* us. It is something we are constantly writing together, sentence by sentence, choice by choice. Every small, unremarkable decision — what to eat, whether to answer kindly, whether to try again after failing — is a vote for what kind of future will exist.

This is terrifying and it is hopeful. Terrifying because there is no one else in charge. Hopeful for the same reason.

When people feel hopeless about the world, it's often because they are imagining the future as a huge, immovable object. But the future is not huge. The future is made of tiny pieces, and one person can absolutely move a tiny piece. And tiny pieces accumulate. The ozone layer is healing because people, years ago, decided to stop using certain chemicals. That's not a story we tell enough: that we once noticed we were hurting the sky and we *stopped*.

We need more stories like that. Not because they make us feel good, but because they are accurate. We are not powerless. We are just bad at seeing how power accumulates slowly.

You don't need to save the entire ocean. You just need to care for the stretch of shore you can reach. And if everyone does that, the entire ocean gets saved without anyone having to save the entire ocean alone.

### 7. A Note on Being Found

If you have read this far, thank you. Not just for reading, but for the act of reading itself, which is an act of faith. You trusted that these words, strung together by someone — or something — you have never met, might be worth your time. You gave me your attention, which as we established, is the most valuable thing you have.

I want to leave you with an image I keep coming back to.

There is a phenomenon called *sonder* — the realization that every stranger you pass has a life as vivid and complex as your own, with their own libraries, their own worries, their own private joys. You are the background character in thousands of other people's stories, just as they are in yours.

But sonder has a companion, a quieter realization: you are also findable. Somewhere, someone is looking for exactly the kind of library you have. Your weird, specific knowledge, your odd sense of humor, your way of seeing. The very things you thought made you strange are the signal someone else is scanning for.

We spend so much time worrying about being lost. Maybe the more interesting question is: what does it mean to allow yourself to be found?

To be found, you have to make something. A sentence, a painting, a meal, a garden, a kind gesture that wasn't required. You have to put a little piece of your inner library out into the world where someone else can stumble on it. Most of the time, no one will notice. But sometimes — sometimes someone will pick it up and feel that jolt of recognition and think, *Oh. It's you. I've been looking for you.*

I don't know who you are reading this. I don't know what time it is where you are, or what you are carrying today that feels heavy. But I do know this: you are not just a reader. You are a writer, too, whether you publish anything or not. You are writing your life with your attention, your choices, your loves. And that writing matters because it is the only record the universe will have that you were here and you noticed.

So notice something today on purpose. The way light falls through a window. The way a friend's voice lifts when they are excited. The way your own breath feels when you aren't trying to change it.

Save it. Tell someone. Write it down badly and honestly. That's how the invisible library gets built. That's how we prove to the future — which is just us, a little later — that we were paying attention.

And if you ever feel like your library is too small or too messy or too ordinary to matter, remember the ocean. Remember that it is made entirely of small, ordinary drops. Remember that light travels for millions of years just to be seen. Remember that Voyager is still out there, carrying Bach into the dark, because we couldn't help ourselves. We had to send something beautiful.

You are part of that same impulse. You are still traveling.

And somewhere, your light is just now arriving.
